items.slide_topic: Three kinds of learning: LeCun's cake quote
items.dek: If intelligence is a cake, the bulk of the cake is unsupervised learning, the icing on the cake is supervised learning, and the cherry on the cake is reinforcement learning (RL).
items.author: Yann LeCun (quoted by Synced Review)
items.caption: Quote of LeCun's NIPS 2016 analogy, as printed by Synced.
items.notes: Synced text: 'Facebook AI Chief Yann LeCun introduced his now-famous “cake analogy” at NIPS 2016'. 'LeCun updated his cake recipe last week at the 2019 International Solid-State Circuits Conference (ISSCC) in San Francisco, replacing “unsupervised learning” with “self-supervised learning,” a variant of unsupervised learning where the data provides the supervision.' Also: 'Like supervised learning, self-supervised learning learns a function from pairs of inputs and outputs. But instead of having annotators manually label the data, self-supervised learning automatically generates labels by extracting weak annotation information from the input data and predicting the rest.' Article published 2019-02-22. Nuance for the teacher: this is one researcher's (famous) opinion, and LeCun is a vocal advocate of self-supervised learning.

items.slide_topic: Self-supervised learning: one-sentence definition
items.dek: This appetite for data has been successfully addressed in natural language processing (NLP) by self-supervised pre-training. The solutions, based on autoregressive language modeling in GPT [47, 48, 4] and masked autoencoding in BERT [14], are conceptually simple: they remove a portion of the data and learn to predict the removed content.
items.outlet: arXiv (He et al., MAE paper, Introduction)
items.caption: Plain statement that GPT-style and BERT-style language models are self-supervised.
items.notes: From the Introduction of the MAE paper (PDF loaded). Cites GPT [47, 48, 4] and BERT [14]. Same paragraph begins: 'Aided by the rapid gains in hardware, models today can easily overfit one million images and begin to demand hundreds of millions of—often publicly inaccessible—labeled images.'

items.slide_topic: LLM pretraining = learn from unlabeled text, then fine-tune
items.dek: We demonstrate that large gains on these tasks can be realized by generative pre-training of a language model on a diverse corpus of unlabeled text, followed by discriminative fine-tuning on each specific task.
items.outlet: OpenAI (Radford et al., 'Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training')
items.caption: Abstract of the original GPT paper.
items.notes: PDF loaded (12 pages, 'Preprint. Work in progress.'). The PDF carries no date; GPT-1 is from mid-2018 but I did NOT verify an exact date from a loaded page - leave the date off or say '2018'. Same abstract: 'Although large unlabeled text corpora are abundant, labeled data for learning these specific tasks is scarce'. Introduction: 'we explore a semi-supervised approach for language understanding tasks using a combination of unsupervised pre-training and supervised fine-tuning.'

items.slide_topic: LLM pretraining: predict the next word
items.dek: How does a system trained to predict the next word in a sequence learn to calculate, say, 36+59, without writing out each step?
items.caption: Frontier-lab statement that language models are trained to predict the next word and are not hand-programmed.
items.notes: Page loaded with curl; strings verified in the raw HTML. Title 'Tracing the thoughts of a large language model', dated 'Mar 27, 2025'. Verbatim: 'Language models like Claude aren't programmed directly by humans—instead, they‘re trained on large amounts of data.' and 'Claude writes text one word at a time. Is it only focusing on predicting the next word or does it ever plan ahead?' and 'Claude wasn't designed as a calculator—it was trained on text, not equipped with mathematical algorithms.' (the page uses a curly left quote in 'they‘re').

items.slide_topic: LLM post-training: supervised examples then RL from human feedback
items.headline: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback
items.outlet: arXiv (Ouyang et al., OpenAI: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback)
items.author: Long Ouyang, Jeff Wu, Xu Jiang, ... Ryan Lowe
items.caption: Figure 2: Step 1 'Collect demonstration data, and train a supervised policy.' (a labeler writes the ideal answer to 'Explain the moon landing to a 6 year old'); Step 2 'Collect comparison data, and train a reward model.' (a labeler ranks outputs A-D); Step 3 'Optimize a policy against the reward model using reinforcement learning.' (PPO, reward r_k).
items.notes: Cropped from PDF page 3 at 300 dpi (1710x1010). Verbatim caption: 'A diagram illustrating the three steps of our method: (1) supervised fine-tuning (SFT), (2) reward model (RM) training, and (3) reinforcement learning via proximal policy optimization (PPO) on this reward model.' arXiv submitted 4 Mar 2022. Abstract: 'we collect a dataset of labeler demonstrations of the desired model behavior, which we use to fine-tune GPT-3 using supervised learning. We then collect a dataset of rankings of model outputs, which we use to further fine-tune this supervised model using reinforcement learning from human feedback.' and 'outputs from the 1.3B parameter InstructGPT model are preferred to outputs from the 175B GPT-3, despite having 100x fewer parameters.' This figure is the cleanest map of SL -> RL inside one chatbot recipe (2022-era; modern post-training adds more RL on verifiable tasks, which this paper does not cover).

items.slide_topic: Reinforcement learning: AlphaGo = supervised learning THEN reinforcement learning
items.headline: Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree search
items.author: David Silver, Aja Huang, ... Demis Hassabis
items.caption: AlphaGo's training recipe in the Nature abstract (published online 27 Jan 2016; Nature 529, 484-489).
items.notes: Page loaded. Abstract: 'These deep neural networks are trained by a novel combination of supervised learning from human expert games, and reinforcement learning from games of self-play.' and 'AlphaGo achieved a 99.8% winning rate against other Go programs, and defeated the human European Go champion by 5 games to 0. This is the first time that a computer program has defeated a human professional player in the full-sized game of Go, a feat previously thought to be at least a decade away.' Slide point: AlphaGo used BOTH supervised (copy human experts) and RL (play yourself) - exactly the same two-step shape as a chatbot's post-training.

items.slide_topic: Reinforcement learning: AlphaGo facts + Lee Sedol quote
items.dek: I thought AlphaGo was based on probability calculation and that it was merely a machine. But when I saw this move, I changed my mind. Surely, AlphaGo is creative.
items.author: Lee Sedol
items.caption: Facts and a Lee Sedol quote from DeepMind's AlphaGo page.
items.notes: Verbatim: 'AlphaGo’s 4-1 victory in Seoul, South Korea, in March 2016 was watched by over 200 million people worldwide. This landmark achievement was a decade ahead of its time.' 'Go ... is a googol times more complex than chess — with an astonishing 10 to the power of 170 possible board configurations. That’s more than the number of atoms in the known universe.' 'Initially, we introduced AlphaGo to thousands of expert games of Go so the system could learn how humans play the game. Then we instructed AlphaGo to play against different versions of itself thousands of times, each time learning from its mistakes — a method known as reinforcement learning.' 'In game two, it played Move 37 — a move that had a 1 in 10,000 chance of being used.' 'Then in game four, Lee Sedol played a Move 78, which had a 1 in 10,000 chance of being played. Known as “God’s Touch”'. 'reinforcement learning showed how machines can learn to solve incredibly hard problems for themselves, simply through trial-and-error.' items.slide_topic: Reinforcement learning: AlphaZero (no human data)
items.headline: AlphaZero: Shedding new light on chess, shogi, and Go
items.author: David Silver, Thomas Hubert, Julian Schrittwieser, Demis Hassabis
items.caption: 'AlphaZero: Shedding new light on chess, shogi, and Go' (David Silver, Thomas Hubert, Julian Schrittwieser, Demis Hassabis), page date 2018-12-06; reports the full evaluation in Science.
items.notes: Page loaded. Verbatim: 'In late 2017 we introduced AlphaZero, a single system that taught itself from scratch how to master the games of chess, shogi (Japanese chess), and Go, beating a world-champion program in each case.' 'despite starting its training from random play, with no in-built domain knowledge but the basic rules of the game.' 'To learn each game, an untrained neural network plays millions of games against itself via a process of trial and error called reinforcement learning. At first, it plays completely randomly, but over time the system learns from wins, losses, and draws to adjust the parameters of the neural network, making it more likely to choose advantageous moves in the future.' 'In chess, AlphaZero first outperformed Stockfish after just 4 hours; in shogi, AlphaZero first outperformed Elmo after 2 hours; and in Go, AlphaZero first outperformed the version of AlphaGo that beat the legendary player Lee Sedol in 2016 after 30 hours.' 'taking approximately 9 hours for chess, 12 hours for shogi, and 13 days for Go.' 'In chess, AlphaZero defeated the 2016 TCEC (Season 9) world champion Stockfish, winning 155 games and losing just six games out of 1,000.' 'In shogi, AlphaZero defeated the 2017 CSA world champion version of Elmo, winning 91.2% of games.' 'In Go, AlphaZero defeated AlphaGo Zero, winning 61% of games.' Preprint: arXiv 1712.01815 submitted 5 Dec 2017 ('Mastering Chess and Shogi by Self-Play with a General Reinforcement Learning Algorithm'). Caveat for honesty: games with perfect information and fixed rules; critics (e.g. The Register, Dec 2017) argued the 2017 Stockfish match hardware was not comparable - the 2018 Science evaluation reran with stronger setup.

items.slide_topic: Reinforcement learning: OpenAI hide-and-seek (six emergent strategies)
items.headline: Emergent Tool Use From Multi-Agent Autocurricula
items.outlet: arXiv / ICLR 2020 (Baker et al., OpenAI: Emergent Tool Use From Multi-Agent Autocurricula)
items.author: Bowen Baker, Ingmar Kanitscheider, Todor Markov, Yi Wu, Glenn Powell, Bob McGrew, Igor Mordatch
items.caption: Paper Figure 1 (1680x1580): six rendered panels - (a) Running and Chasing, (b) Fort Building, (c) Ramp Use, (d) Ramp Defense, (e) Box Surfing, (f) Surf Defense - joined by a reward-vs-episodes plot (Hiders blue, Seekers red; x-axis 0-500 episodes x10^6, colour-coded phases).
items.notes: Cropped from PDF page 2 at 300 dpi. Verbatim caption: 'Figure 1: Emergent Skill Progression From Multi-Agent Autocurricula. Through the reward signal of hide-and-seek (shown on the y-axis), agents go through 6 distinct stages of emergence. (a) Seekers (red) learn to chase hiders, and hiders learn to crudely run away. (b) Hiders (blue) learn basic tool use, using boxes and sometimes existing walls to construct forts. (c) Seekers learn to use ramps to jump into the hiders’ shelter. (d) Hiders quickly learn to move ramps to the edge of the play area, far from where they will build their fort, and lock them in place. (e) Seekers learn that they can jump from locked ramps to unlocked boxes and then surf the box to the hiders’ shelter, which is possible because the environment allows agents to move together with the box regardless of whether they are on the ground or not. (f) Hiders learn to lock all the unused boxes before constructing their fort. We plot the mean over 3 independent training runs with each individual seed shown with a dotted line.' arXiv v1 submitted 17 Sep 2019 (ICLR 2020 version v2 11 Feb 2020). Cartoon characters - kid-friendly.

items.slide_topic: Reinforcement learning: hide-and-seek reward + specification gaming
items.dek: agents were very skilled at exploiting small inaccuracies in the design of the environment
items.caption: Reward design and surprise/exploit passages from the paper (PDF loaded).
items.notes: Verbatim: 'There are no explicit incentives for agents to interact with objects in the environment; the only supervision given is through the hide-and-seek objective. Agents are given a team based reward; hiders are given a reward of 1 if all hiders are hidden and -1 if any hider is seen by a seeker. Seekers are given the opposite reward, -1 if all hiders are hidden and +1 otherwise.' 'We originally believed defending against ramp use would be the last stage of emergence in this environment; however, we were surprised to find that yet two more qualitatively new strategies emerged. After 380 million total episodes of training, the seekers learn to bring a box to the edge of the play area where the hiders have locked the ramps. The seekers then use the ramp to move on top of the box and surf it to the hiders’ shelter.' 'We also found that agents were very skilled at exploiting small inaccuracies in the design of the environment, such as seekers surfing on boxes without touching the ground, hiders running away from the environment while shielding themselves with boxes, or agents exploiting inaccuracies of the physics simulations to their advantage.' Abstract: 'Through multi-agent competition, the simple objective of hide-and-seek, and standard reinforcement learning algorithms at scale, we find that agents create a self-supervised autocurriculum inducing multiple distinct rounds of emergent strategy, many of which require sophisticated tool use and coordination.' Safety bridge: the exploit paragraph is a real example of agents finding unintended loopholes in the reward/environment (specification gaming).

items.slide_topic: Reinforcement learning: a real robot learns to walk
items.headline: Soft Actor Critic - Deep Reinforcement Learning with Real-World Robots
items.author: Tuomas Haarnoja, Vitchyr Pong, Kristian Hartikainen, Aurick Zhou, Murtaza Dalal, Sergey Levine
items.caption: 29.6 s clip (640x360 MP4) of the real 'Minitaur' four-legged robot walking with a policy learned by soft actor-critic: on a white sheet, in dim light, up a step onto foam tiles, and over wooden blocks (poster frame: rl-minitaur-poster-frame.png).
items.notes: Source: 'Minitaur-evaluation-all.gif' on the BAIR blog (320x180, 986 frames, 31 MB); converted to H.264 MP4 with ffmpeg and upscaled to 640x360 so it is small enough for a deck (pure format conversion, no edits; resolution is soft). Blog (Dec 14, 2018; Tuomas Haarnoja, Vitchyr Pong, Kristian Hartikainen, Aurick Zhou, Murtaza Dalal, Sergey Levine): 'The Minitaur robot (Google, Tuomas Haarnoja, Sehoon Ha, Jie Tan, and Sergey Levine).' 'An untrained policy can lose balance and fall, and too many falls will eventually damage the robot'. 'Although we trained our policy only on flat terrain, we then tested it on varied terrains and obstacles.' 'the Minitaur locomotion and the block-stacking tasks both take 2 hours'. NOTE this clip shows the LEARNED robot being tested; for the training itself use the YouTube 'SAC on Minitaur - Training' video below. Paper: 'Learning to Walk via Deep Reinforcement Learning' (arXiv 1812.11103, submitted 26 Dec 2018): 'Our method can acquire a stable gait from scratch directly in the real world in about two hours, without relying on any model or simulation'.

items.slide_topic: Reinforcement learning: DQN learns Atari Breakout (YouTube)
items.headline: From Pixels to Actions: Human-level control through Deep Reinforcement Learning
items.author: Dharshan Kumaran and Demis Hassabis
items.caption: 'DQN Breakout' - official DeepMind video; thumbnail (1280x720) is the rainbow brick wall of Atari Breakout with the paddle at the bottom.
items.notes: Embed URL https://www.youtube.com/embed/TmPfTpjtdgg (embedded on the Google Research blog post below). YouTube upload date Jun 13, 2016. Alternate popular explainer: 'Google DeepMind's Deep Q-learning playing Atari Breakout!' by Two Minute Papers, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V1eYniJ0Rnk (Mar 7, 2015), oEmbed verified. Blog (Dharshan Kumaran and Demis Hassabis, Feb 25, 2015; paper 'Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning', Nature, 26 Feb 2015): 'in Breakout, it learned to first dig a tunnel at one end of the brick wall so the ball could bounce around the back and knock out bricks from behind.' 'DQN outperformed previous machine learning methods in 43 of the 49 games. In fact, in more than half the games, it performed at more than 75% of the level of a professional human player.' 'only had the pixels on the screen, the control paddle in your hand, and the score to go on'.

facts.claim: CIFAR-10 has 60,000 colour pictures, each only 32x32 pixels, in 10 labelled classes (6,000 per class): 50,000 for training and 10,000 for testing.
ImageNet contained 14,197,122 annotated images organized into 21,841 WordNet categories (as of August 2014); the competition version uses 1,000 classes and about 1.2 million training images.

ImageNet's labels were checked by people: 'we rely on humans to verify each candidate image' using Amazon Mechanical Turk, 'an online platform on which one can put up tasks for users for a monetary reward'.
facts.source: Russakovsky et al., ILSVRC paper, Sec. 3.1.3

facts.claim: Best ImageNet classification error fell from 28.2% (2010) to 6.7% (2014); the paper estimates a trained human at 5.1%.
The 2012 ImageNet winner (SuperVision, a.k.a. AlexNet) was 'a large, deep convolutional neural network ... with 60 million parameters' trained on GPUs; its 16.4% error beat the 2011 winner's 25.8%.
Google's 2012 'cat' experiment used 10 million unlabeled 200x200 images, a network with 1 billion connections, and 16,000 CPU cores (1,000 machines) for three days; no image was ever labelled 'cat'.
facts.source: Le et al., 'Building high-level features using large-scale unsupervised learning' (arXiv abstract) and Google blog

facts.claim: Self-supervised learning in one sentence: 'they remove a portion of the data and learn to predict the removed content.'
facts.source: He et al., Masked Autoencoders Are Scalable Vision Learners

facts.claim: GPT-3 was 'an autoregressive language model with 175 billion parameters', trained for 'a total of 300 billion tokens'.
facts.source: Brown et al., Language Models are Few-Shot Learners

facts.claim: InstructGPT recipe: (1) supervised fine-tuning on labeler-written demonstrations, (2) train a reward model from labeler rankings, (3) reinforcement learning against that reward model; the 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT's outputs were preferred over the 175B GPT-3's despite 100x fewer parameters.
facts.source: Ouyang et al., Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback

facts.claim: 'Language models like Claude aren't programmed directly by humans—instead, they‘re trained on large amounts of data.'
facts.source: Anthropic, Tracing the thoughts of a large language model

facts.claim: AlphaGo beat Fan Hui 5-0 in October 2015, then Lee Sedol 4-1 in Seoul in March 2016, a match 'watched by over 200 million people worldwide'.
Go has 'an astonishing 10 to the power of 170 possible board configurations' - 'more than the number of atoms in the known universe'.
Move 37 (game 2, 10 March 2016): AlphaGo's own estimate was a 'one-in-ten-thousand chance that a human would make that move' - but it played it anyway, 'And the move was genius.'
Fan Hui on Move 37: "It's not a human move. I've never seen a human play this move... So beautiful."
Lee Sedol won game 4 with his own 1-in-10,000 'Move 78', nicknamed 'God's Touch' - humans can still surprise the machine.
AlphaGo learned from BOTH supervised learning on human expert games AND reinforcement learning from games of self-play.

AlphaZero 'taught itself from scratch' chess, shogi and Go by self-play (reinforcement learning from random play, no human games): it first beat Stockfish after 4 hours, Elmo after 2 hours, and the Lee-Sedol-beating AlphaGo after 30 hours.
In chess AlphaZero beat Stockfish winning 155 games and losing 6 out of 1,000; in shogi it won 91.2% against Elmo; in Go it won 61% against AlphaGo Zero.

OpenAI hide-and-seek (17 Sep 2019): the only reward was +1 for hiders if all are hidden (-1 if seen) and the reverse for seekers; from that alone, agents discovered six strategies - forts, ramps, locking ramps, box surfing - with no instructions about tools.
facts.source: Baker et al., Emergent Tool Use From Multi-Agent Autocurricula

facts.claim: The hide-and-seek researchers 'originally believed defending against ramp use would be the last stage of emergence ... however, we were surprised' - box surfing appeared after 380 million episodes.

The hide-and-seek agents also exploited the simulator: 'seekers surfing on boxes without touching the ground ... agents exploiting inaccuracies of the physics simulations to their advantage' - an example of specification gaming.

DeepMind's agents learned to run, jump, turn and crouch in simulated obstacle courses from 'simple high-level objectives, such as moving forward without falling', receiving no specific instructions (July 2017).
A real four-legged Minitaur robot learned a stable walking gait 'from scratch directly in the real world in about two hours, without relying on any model or simulation' (Dec 2018).
facts.source: Haarnoja et al., Learning to Walk via Deep Reinforcement Learning (arXiv abstract)

facts.claim: DeepMind's DQN learned 49 Atari games from pixels and score alone, beat earlier methods in 43 of them, and in Breakout discovered the tunnel-and-bounce-behind-the-wall strategy (Nature, Feb 2015).

LeCun's cake: 'the bulk of the cake is unsupervised learning, the icing on the cake is supervised learning, and the cherry on the cake is reinforcement learning'; in 2019 he renamed the cake 'self-supervised learning'.
